steps.title: Apply online for your study permit (temporary resident visa included)
steps.why: You need a study permit to study at UBC, and you should apply before you travel to Canada. Because your citizenship requires a visitor visa, IRCC issues the temporary resident visa together with your study permit approval — there's no separate application and no extra fee, but allow extra time because your passport must be sent in for the visa to be placed in it before you travel. Processing times vary by country, so apply as soon as you accept your offer.
prerequisites: Accepted UBC offer of admission and letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution (DLI)
An IRCC secure account to pay fees, submit your application, and check status
A scanner or camera to make electronic copies of your documents
A valid credit or debit card
Your local visa office instructions for the country/territory you're applying from
All required supporting documents prepared before you apply
steps.cost: CAN $150 study permit fee (the temporary resident visa is issued with your approval at no additional fee)
steps.time_estimate: Processing times vary by country — check IRCC and apply well before your program start date; add extra time for your passport to be submitted and returned with the visa

steps.title: Book and give your biometrics (fingerprints and photo)
steps.why: IRCC collects biometrics for most study permit applications to confirm your identity and help assess your application. After you apply, you'll receive a biometric instruction letter — you have 30 days to give your biometrics, and booking your collection appointment as soon as you can avoids processing delays. Once given, biometrics are valid for 10 years, making repeat trips to Canada easier.
prerequisites: Submitted study permit application online through IRCC
Paid the biometrics fee at the time you submitted your application
Received the letter from IRCC telling you to give biometrics
steps.cost: CAN$85 per individual applicant; maximum CAN$170 total for families applying at the same time (spouse/common-law partner and dependent children)
steps.time_estimate: Must be completed within 30 days of receiving the biometrics instruction letter

steps.title: Book and complete your immigration medical exam with an IRCC panel physician
steps.why: Only physicians authorized by IRCC can perform an immigration medical exam (IME), and you must be in good health to be admitted to Canada on a study permit. Booking early avoids delays, since results must be sent to the office processing your application — your own family doctor cannot do the exam unless they appear on IRCC's panel physician list.
prerequisites: Study permit application submitted (or IRCC instruction/medical request letter received)
Valid passport or travel document to present at the appointment
Know which visa office is processing your application, so the panel physician sends results to the right office
Use IRCC's list of panel physicians to find an authorized doctor in your area (you may choose one anywhere in the world)
steps.cost: Paid by you; the fee varies from one panel physician to another
steps.time_estimate: Book as early as possible — appointment plus time for the physician to transmit results to IRCC before you travel

steps.title: Arrange your international funds transfer early for Term 1 tuition (due September 9, 2026)
steps.why: Your Term 1 Winter Session tuition — covering Term 1 courses, the first half of two-term courses, and most student fees — is due September 9, 2026, and your exact assessed amounts appear under "Finances" in Workday. Because you are paying from a restricted or less liquid currency corridor, expect longer transfer lead times, fewer providers, and possible exchange-control paperwork, so begin the transfer well before the deadline. Also confirm whether your home country or funding programme imposes its own proof-of-funds or outbound-payment requirements in addition to UBC's, and budget for the other charges hitting your account: the $3,000 acceptance deposit for students on a study permit (deadline between May 1 and June 1, per your letter of admission or the Applicant Service Centre), the temporary iMED insurance fee of $237 ($338 for one-term exchange students) plus a $10.54 direct billing fee charged when you register, and residence/meal plan instalments due September 19, 2026 and January 9, 2027 if you live on campus.
prerequisites: Accepted your offer of admission
Registered for courses so tuition and iMED fees are assessed
Access to Workday to view assessed fees under "Finances"
Checked your home country's outbound-payment or exchange-control requirements and any funding programme conditions
steps.cost: Tuition as assessed in Workday (use UBC's cost estimator for an estimate); iMED $237 or $338 plus $10.54 direct billing fee; plus any transfer fees or exchange costs charged by your provider
steps.time_estimate: Start several weeks before the September 9, 2026 deadline; 1–2 hours to set up plus transfer processing time

steps.title: Prepare your port-of-entry documents and clear the border
steps.why: Your approval letter is not your study permit — you receive the actual study permit from a border services officer at the port of entry. The officer will confirm you meet basic entry requirements, so you must be able to hand over the right documents on the spot or you risk delays or being refused entry.
prerequisites: Study permit application approved and port of entry letter of introduction received (contains your permit reference number)
Valid travel document such as a passport — the same passport you used to apply for your study permit

Valid eTA (linked to that passport), valid visitor visa (temporary resident visa) in your passport, valid green card or equivalent proof of U.S. status, or another valid travel document, if you need one
Copy of your valid UBC letter of acceptance (an updated LOA plus a valid letter of introduction if you deferred your enrolment)
Letters of reference or any other documents the visa office told you to bring
Proof of enough money for your stay
Read the pre-departure guide and the CBSA information for international students
steps.cost: No fee at the port of entry
steps.time_estimate: Assemble documents before departure; border processing on arrival

steps.title: Apply for your Social Insurance Number (SIN) with Service Canada
steps.why: A SIN is the 9-digit number you need to work in Canada — on or off campus — and to open most types of bank accounts and access government benefits and credit payments. As a temporary resident, your SIN starts with "9" and expires with your immigration documents, so you'll need to apply again to extend the expiry date when your study permit is renewed. Applying online gives faster processing; have all required documents ready before you start, because if you make a mistake or forget a document you cannot go back — you must submit an entirely new application with all documents again. Protect your SIN as soon as it's issued: it is private, illegal for anyone else to use, and misuse can lead to identity theft or loss of tax refunds and benefits. If Service Canada cannot issue you a SIN, you may instead request a temporary tax number (TTN) from the CRA.
prerequisites: Be 12 years or older (anyone 12+ can apply for their own SIN)
One primary identity document proving your legal status in Canada (as a temporary resident, your study permit / immigration document)
One secondary identity document confirming your identity (e.g. passport)
Supporting documents if your name has changed, and certified translations if a document is not in English or French
Confirm any errors on your documents are corrected by the issuing source before applying
steps.time_estimate: About 30 minutes to complete the online application; apply online for faster processing
applies_to_rules: Temporary residents: SIN begins with "9" and expires with your immigration documents — reapply to extend the expiry date
Application details that don't match your primary identity document will be recorded as they appear on that document
Service Canada no longer issues plastic SIN cards; view and print your SIN through My Service Canada Account (MSCA)

steps.title: Apply for BC's Medical Services Plan (MSP) as soon as you arrive in B.C.
steps.why: All B.C. residents must enrol in the Medical Services Plan (MSP), and if you don't have other medical coverage you are required by B.C. law to register. If you're new to Canada, apply as soon as you arrive: your coverage may only start three months after your arrival date in British Columbia, so applying late pushes your coverage start date back. Applying online is the easiest and fastest way to enrol. Enrolment also gets you your Personal Health Number (PHN) via the B.C. Services Card process. During the three-month wait period you need private health care insurance — as a UBC international student, temporary iMED medical insurance is charged to your account when you register for courses and covers you until your MSP coverage begins (likely in November if you arrived in August). Note that coverage depends on residency: if you leave B.C. within 6 months of enrolling for MSP, you may have to repay your medical expenses.
prerequisites: Arrived in British Columbia and established residence
Registered for UBC courses (triggers the temporary iMED insurance fee that bridges the MSP wait period)
Proof of your arrival date in B.C. and immigration/study permit documents for the online MSP application
steps.cost: MSP premiums: $0 for Canadian citizens and permanent residents; $75/month for students on a study permit. Interim iMED coverage: $237 (or $338 for one-term exchange students), plus a $10.54 direct billing fee.
steps.time_estimate: Apply online as soon as you arrive; MSP coverage begins about three months after your arrival date in B.C. (e.g., an August arrival is typically covered from November 1, 2026 onward)

steps.title: Check your MSP application status and confirm when coverage starts
steps.why: Everyone residing in B.C. must enrol in the Medical Services Plan (MSP) to access provincial health benefits like doctor visits, but coverage does not start immediately. New residents must complete a wait period equal to the balance of the month in which residence is established plus two months — if you are new to Canada, coverage may start about three months after your arrival date in B.C. Following up now confirms your application is progressing and tells you exactly how long you must rely on private insurance, so you are not left uninsured. Note that coverage depends on residency: if you leave B.C. within 6 months of enrolling, you may have to repay your medical expenses.
prerequisites: A submitted Application for MSP Enrolment (online, in person or by mail — online is the easiest and fastest)
Your date of arrival in British Columbia, which determines the start of your wait period
The ID you used to apply (ID requirements apply to MSP enrolment)
Private health care insurance arranged to cover you during the wait period
If moving from another province: continued coverage under your former provincial medical plan during the wait period
If your coverage is under an employer, union or pension group plan: your group administrator's contact details, since they handle applying
steps.cost: No application fee is listed in the sources; budget separately for private health insurance during the wait period
steps.time_estimate: Short follow-up (online, in person or by mail); coverage itself begins only after the wait period — the balance of your month of arrival plus two months (roughly three months after arrival)
